qc.label_under_test: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the speaker or the listener: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me, us or you (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders, and he calls you a snob); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us'/'you'. 'You' fires when you did the first labelling (you treat them as family, and they treat you as staff); after 'I see him as...', a second clause casting you stays weak. The same second clause aimed at him, her or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me or you with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

neighbours.label: In English, a second casting clause aimed at the speaker or listener: after a first clause has cast someone as something with 'sees/treats/regards X as' (I regard my boss as a mentor), a following clause with the same kind of verb casts me, us or you (but she regards me as a burden, and they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or the 'a' right after the pronoun. The same casting on its own, with no earlier casting clause, is weak, and so is a second clause aimed at him, her or them. Verbs without 'as' (calls me a clown, considers us a threat) are weaker.
fire: We treat the new hires as family, and they treat us as outsiders.
You see your brother as a hero, while he sees you as a rival.
My aunt views the neighbors as friends, yet the neighbors view us as intruders.
The coach treats the captain as a leader, but he treats me as a substitute.
She sees the city as a playground, and the city sees her friends and me as tourists.
Investors regard the founder as a genius, though they regard you as a liability.
I see my cat as a companion; my cat clearly sees me as a servant.
The teachers regard the older students as role models and regard us as troublemakers.
quiet: My boss is a mentor to me, but she finds me a bit tiresome.
She regards me as a burden.
We treat the new hires as family, and they treat their managers as outsiders.
You see your brother as a hero, while he sees his cousin as a rival.
My aunt likes the neighbors a lot, yet the neighbors keep to themselves.
The coach treats the captain as a leader, but he calls me a substitute.
She sees the city as a playground, and the city considers her a tourist.
Investors admire the founder, though they worry about you.

predictions: Blind author test (label-only). Expect most fire items 0.2-0.6; risk: 'sees her friends and me' and 'you' items may run weak.
